definition.text: A historical argument is an interpretation of the past supported by evidence drawn from primary sources.

anchor.quote: an interpretation of the past supported by evidence drawn from primary sources

facts.text: Historians justify claims with evidence, using contextual reasoning to connect the sources to the interpretation.

anchor.quote: using contextual reasoning to connect the sources to the interpretation

facts.text: Every historical argument is bounded by the limitations of the surviving record, which is always incomplete.

anchor.quote: bounded by the limitations of the surviving record, which is always incomplete

misconceptions.text: Students treat a forceful assertion about the past as an argument, without connecting it to primary-source evidence or naming the record's gaps.
misconceptions.corrective: An argument links a claim to evidence through reasoning and states what the evidence cannot settle.

examples.text: A claim about a revolt's causes must rest on letters, records, or accounts, noting whose voices the record omits.

mcBank.stem: What distinguishes a historical argument from a mere assertion about the past?
options: It links a claim to primary-source evidence through reasoning
It states the conclusion more confidently
It avoids citing any specific sources

mapping.claim: a historical interpretation of the past
mapping.warrant: contextual reasoning connecting the sources to the interpretation
mapping.limitation: the gaps and bias in the surviving record

definition.text: In historical method, a primary source is evidence about its maker and moment as much as its ostensible subject.

anchor.quote: a primary source is evidence about its maker and moment as much as its ostensible subject

facts.text: Source criticism asks who created the source, when, why, and for whom before asking what it reports.

anchor.quote: Source criticism asks who created the source, when, why, and for whom before asking what it reports

facts.text: Provenance and bias bound the claims any one document can support.

anchor.quote: provenance and bias bound the claims any one document can support

misconceptions.text: Students read a primary source as a transparent window onto the past, ignoring how its author's purpose and audience shape what it can support.
misconceptions.corrective: Ask who made the source, when, for whom, and why before asking what it says.

examples.text: A general's victory dispatch is strong evidence of how he wanted the battle remembered, and weaker evidence of what actually happened on the field.

mcBank.stem: Before using a primary source as evidence, a historian first asks
options: who made it, when, and for what purpose
whether it agrees with the course textbook
whether it is written in the original language
how many total pages the document runs

mapping.maker and context: who created it, when, and why
mapping.what it can support: the historical claims it can support

definition.text: Contextual interpretation reads a historical source by moving between the detail and its context: each detail is understood in light of the broader period, and the historian's picture of the period is revised as more details come to light.

anchor.quote: each detail is understood in light of the broader period, and the historian's picture of the period is revised as more details come to light

facts.text: A claim about the past earns support when specific evidence is situated in its context, not when details are listed in isolation.

anchor.quote: A claim about the past earns support when specific evidence is situated in its context

facts.text: Understanding emerges from the circle between the particular source and the whole era.

anchor.quote: Understanding emerges from the circle between the particular source and the whole era

misconceptions.text: Students judge a past detail by present-day standards instead of situating it in the context of its own period.
misconceptions.corrective: Read each detail in light of the period it belongs to before drawing a claim about the past.

examples.text: A single inventory entry means little until it is situated in the trade patterns of its decade, which reshape what the whole archive shows.

mcBank.stem: Situating a historical detail in its context means reading it in light of
options: the broader period it belongs to
whichever interpretation is most popular today
the alphabetical order of the archive's folders
a fixed assumption that all sources mean one thing

mapping.work: the historical record of a period
